articles.title: Harvard’s tiny UV light chip could help shrink quantum computers
articles.summary: Harvard-led researchers have developed a microscopic device that generates 120 times more ultraviolet light than previous comparable approaches by efficiently converting red light into UV. The breakthrough could unlock smaller quantum computers, ultra-precise atomic clocks, and compact environmental sensors.
articles.content:
Ultraviolet (UV) light is already essential to a wide range of modern technologies. Beyond its natural presence in sunlight, it is used to disinfect surfaces, make biological materials fluoresce, and manufacture computer chips through a process called photolithography. In the future, microscopic sources of UV light built directly into photonic chips could enable smaller quantum computers, ultra-precise atomic clocks, and other advanced technologies.

However, shrinking UV light sources to fit on a chip has presented a significant engineering challenge. Ultraviolet light rapidly loses power as it travels through optical waveguides, the tiny channels that carry light across a chip. This limitation has made it extremely difficult to develop compact UV sources with enough power for practical applications.

Now, a Harvard-led research team has demonstrated a microscopic photonic device that produces approximately 120 times more UV power than previous comparable devices. The researchers, working in the laboratory of Marko Lončar, the Tiantsai Lin Professor of Electrical Engineering, achieved the breakthrough using a widely studied material called thin-film lithium niobate.

Published in Nature Communications, the findings establish lithium niobate as a promising platform for generating powerful ultraviolet light in compact devices while minimizing optical losses.

Turning Red Light Into Ultraviolet Light

Rather than trying to deliver ultraviolet light directly through microscopic channels, the researchers designed a device that generates UV light from red light within the chip itself.

The approach relies on a process known as frequency upconversion. Inside the lithium niobate crystal, two photons of red light combine to produce a single ultraviolet photon with higher energy. Lithium niobate is particularly well suited to this process because of its exceptional ability to convert light from one frequency to another.

"Our group is perhaps best known for utilizing lithium niobate for photonic devices that operate at longer, infrared wavelengths -- closer to the realm of telecommunications signals," Lončar said.

However, the team found that this transparent crystalline material, which has become increasingly important in integrated photonics, can also support light sources and guide light at much shorter wavelengths, including those in the ultraviolet range.

"When people think about [thin-film lithium niobate], they don't think of it as a UV material, but we show that it is," said co-first author Kees Franken, former research fellow in the Lončar lab. "We also show that there are some other nonlinear effects happening that we don't fully understand yet."

A New Technique Overcomes a Major Engineering Barrier

The device uses optical waveguides, microscopic channels etched into the lithium niobate film that direct light through the chip in much the same way electrical wires carry current.

For red light to be efficiently converted into ultraviolet light, the orientation of regions within the crystal must be repeatedly reversed at precisely controlled intervals along the waveguide. This manufacturing process, called poling, is a specialized technique used in nonlinear optics.

One of the biggest challenges has been creating these patterns with accuracy at scales smaller than a micrometer across devices that extend for centimeters.

Previous manufacturing methods required researchers to make an undesirable compromise. Poling the entire film before forming the waveguides made it difficult to correct manufacturing imperfections. Alternatively, creating the waveguides first reduced conversion efficiency because the electrodes were positioned too far away, allowing only part of the film to be successfully poled.

To eliminate this tradeoff, the Harvard team developed a technique they call "sidewall poling."

Precision Engineering Dramatically Improves Light Conversion

Instead of positioning the electrodes exclusively above the lithium niobate film, the researchers placed precisely patterned metal structures resembling tiny fingers directly alongside the etched waveguide. During fabrication, they applied a small voltage to permanently reverse the orientation of the crystal domains in a carefully controlled pattern.

"The key idea was: could we just put the electrodes directly on the waveguide?" said co-first author and former graduate student Soumya Ghosh. "It's a high-precision fabrication process to position the electrodes but requiring about 50-nanometer accuracy."

This arrangement enabled the researchers to reverse the crystal domains throughout the entire cross section of the waveguide, allowing light traveling through the material to undergo much more efficient frequency conversion.

The team could also fine-tune the spacing of the reversed crystal regions along the device. By incorporating existing "adapted poling" techniques previously developed in Lončar's laboratory and elsewhere, the researchers compensated for variations in the thickness of the lithium niobate film and the shape of the waveguide.

A 120-Fold Increase in Ultraviolet Power

The resulting device generated 4.2 milliwatts of ultraviolet power directly on the chip at a wavelength of 390 nanometers. That represents approximately 120 times the output power achieved by the best previous thin-film lithium niobate devices operating in this wavelength range.

Earlier experiments using the material generated only tens of microwatts of UV power. Although those results demonstrated that the approach was scientifically feasible, the output was too low to support practical applications.

The substantial increase in power could be particularly valuable for trapped-ion quantum computers. These machines use electrically charged atoms to store and process quantum information. Many of the specific atomic energy transitions required to operate them involve light in the near-ultraviolet portion of the spectrum.

"If you want a scalable quantum computer that isn't the size of a truck, you need to scale everything down to the chip level, and this includes the light sources," Franken said.

Beyond Quantum Computing

The technology could also benefit ultra-precise atomic clocks and environmental monitoring systems. According to the researchers, the same range of ultraviolet wavelengths is well suited to compact sensors designed to closely monitor greenhouse gases and other atmospheric pollutants.

Franken and Ghosh attribute the breakthrough partly to the collaborative structure of Lončar's laboratory, where researchers carry out every stage of device development in one place, including theoretical research, engineering design, cleanroom fabrication, and optical testing.

"The hands-on intuition that we gained for how to make a device, while also keeping the zoomed-out view of what this device is for, and how we were going to characterize it -- that's a big part of what enabled this project for us," Ghosh said.

"Milliwatt-level UV generation using sidewall poled lithium niobate" was further co-authored by C.C. Rodrigues, J. Yang, C.J. Xin, S. Lu, D. Witt, G. Joe, G.S. Wiederhecker, and K.-J. Boller.

U.S. federal funding for the project came from the following sources: Department of the Air Force grant No. FA9453-23-C-A039; Office of Naval Research grant No. N00014-22-C-1041/VAS-21-0001; NASA grant No. 80NSSC22K0262 and 80NSSC23PB442; and National Science Foundation grants ERC EEC-1941583 and OMA-2137723.

articles.title: Particles not seen before have been observed in a quantum simulator
articles.summary: Physicists long held that all particles fall under categories of bosons or fermions, but a new experiment offers evidence that a third and long-debated class is possible after all
articles.content:
Physicists long held that all particles fall under categories of bosons or fermions, but a new experiment offers evidence that a third and long-debated class is possible after all

Signatures of paraparticles were seen in a quantum system containing 16 qubits Eli Krantz, Krantz NanoArt

After decades of being dismissed, a group of particles called paraparticles have been seen emerging inside a quantum simulator. Coming only a year after a mathematical breakthrough in our understanding of paraparticles, this experiment complicates our view of the quantum world.

Quantum particles are classified by what happens when two of them swap places and by how many can have the same quantum state simultaneously. Bosons, for example, can be swapped at no penalty, and infinitely many can share a quantum state. Fermions are their opposite; swapping them incurs a change in their quantum states, and two or more fermions can never occupy the same quantum state.

In the 1950s, researchers theorised other types too, but it seemed impossible to experimentally distinguish them from fermions and bosons. But in 2025, Kaden Hazzard at Rice University in Texas and Zhiyuan Wang at the Perimeter Institute in Canada argued that this doesn’t have to be the case.

Advertisement

Their mathematical work made the case for the possibility of finding signs of paraparticles in experiments. Now, Max Hays at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and his colleagues have used a quantum simulator do exactly that.

“They’ve seen emergent paraparticles,” says Hazzard. “They have a system whose dynamics obeys exactly the same mathematical equations that a paraparticle is expected to satisfy.” He says he is surprised by how quickly the team managed to complete this work.

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Lost in Space-Time Sign up to newsletter

The researchers used 16 qubits, which are the building blocks of quantum computers, made from tiny superconducting circuits and arranged in a grid. By using electromagnetic interactions, the team connected qubits into pairs, like rungs on a ladder. Each rung behaved like a paraparticle.

Three tests confirmed this: the researchers swapped two paraparticles, made them crash into each other and, ultimately, checked how they pile together. It all took a year and lots of careful control and calibration of the qubits, says Cora Barrett, also at MIT, who worked on the experiment.

“This work provides a proof of concept that paraparticles are not merely theoretical curiosities,” says Kristian Hauser Villegas at the University of the Philippines Diliman.

Unlike a simulation on a conventional computer, the new experiment uses the qubits’ quantum characters as building blocks of paraparticles, says Hauser Villegas. It may even be impossible to faithfully reproduce this on a conventional computer.

“In a regular computer, you are writing code and it’s very abstract; there’s no way in which these things are actually really existing in the computer,” says Hays. “In this case, you can say the particle is right at this spot physically.”

Going forward, the team wants to expand their experiment to include paraparticles that interact with each other, as well as paraparticles in more complicated geometrical configurations, says Hays.

Many open questions about paraparticles remain, and these more complex experiments will stand a chance of answering some of them, says Wang. “This is the just the beginning of an exciting journey,” he says.

articles.personality_title: Scientists observe a new type of particle in quantum simulator
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Physicists have believed for a long time that all particles belong to two groups: bosons or fermions. These groups behave in specific ways when particles swap places or share energy states. In the 1950s, scientists thought there might be other types, called paraparticles, but no one could prove they exist.

**What happened** – In 2025, two researchers suggested it might be possible to find paraparticles in experiments. Recently, scientists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) used a quantum simulator made of 16 qubits—tiny units in quantum computers—to create conditions where paraparticles could appear. They tested swapping, colliding, and grouping these particles to confirm their behavior matched that of paraparticles.

**Impact** – This experiment is the first clear evidence of paraparticles, showing they are not just theoretical ideas. Unlike regular computer simulations, this quantum simulator physically creates paraparticles, making the discovery more real and reliable. This challenges old ideas about particle types and could change how we understand the quantum world.

**What's next step** – The scientists plan to study paraparticles that interact with each other and explore more complex setups. These future experiments could answer many questions about how these particles behave and what roles they might play in physics and technology.

**One-sentence takeaway** – For the first time, scientists have used a quantum simulator to observe paraparticles, opening a new chapter in understanding the quantum universe.

articles.title: AI solved the hardest problem in maths – is there anything it can’t do?
articles.summary: The past year of solutions to long-standing open problems has shown AI is good at maths, but columnist Jacob Aron says that doesn’t mean it can tackle biology or climate change
articles.content:
The past year of solutions to long-standing open problems has shown AI is good at maths, but columnist Jacob Aron says that doesn’t mean it can tackle biology or climate change

Alzheimer’s disease, involving amyloid plaques in the brain, will be tough for AI to solve JUAN GAERTNER/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY

The progress AI has made in mathematics this year is nothing short of extraordinary. In January, I was impressed to see relatively minor open problems tackled with the help of AI. Now, AI is being used to solve the hardest problems in maths. The obvious next question is, if AI can do this, is there anything it can’t do? That is the inference that the AI companies want us to make, but, in reality, the answer is much more nuanced.

We see this messaging in claims that AI can “solve X”, where X is any field of human endeavour you care to name. Biology is a big one. “Cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, mental illness – these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade,” said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei while promoting the company’s recent initial public offering. “I think one day maybe we can cure all disease with the help of AI,” said Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, last year, adding that this could be “within the next decade or so”.

This phenomenon isn’t new: I call it “physicist brain”, after the propensity for physicists to wade into areas outside their expertise and declare simple solutions. More broadly, it is called Nobel disease, after the many Nobel prizewinners who have gone on to make, shall we say, less evidenced-backed claims. In general, there is a tendency to think that if an intelligent person is good at one thing, they are good at many other things that require intelligence. What is different now is that trillion-dollar companies and large swathes of the global economy now depend on this being true of artificial intelligence.

Advertisement

To be clear, I think we must now admit that AI is better at solving open mathematical problems than any human, and that this has happened faster than anyone ever expected. When I first saw the news in September that the Navier-Stokes problem had been solved by OpenAI, I felt stunned. We had entered a new world. With the announcement of the Riemann hypothesis proof this week, I felt sick and had to go and have a lie-down. These were intellectual Everests I have marvelled at since my teenage years, conquered by a machine far sooner than anyone expected. You may have read my recent piece forecasting the future in 2096 – an early draft had a line, later removed, about three Millennium Prize Problems being solved by AI in the 2030s. We’ve had two this year alone.

But maths isn’t biology. Yes, we have seen advances like AlphaFold, Deepmind’s AI that can predict the structure of proteins, but this is biology at its most mathematical, a computational puzzle. True advances in biology and medicine require studying cells, animals and people, all of which can be frustratingly illogical and uncooperative. Amodei admitted as much in 2024, writing that “the main challenges with directly applying intelligence to biology are data, the speed of the physical world, and intrinsic complexity”. You can imagine mitigations here – AI-directed robotic labs, for example – but it doesn’t seem like we should expect massive speed leaps in capability comparable to those seen in mathematics. There isn’t an easy way to confirm that a biological discovery is correct, in the manner that the computer code Lean allows for mathematics.

Worse still are claims that AI will “solve climate change”. For Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, this came as a throwaway comment in a 2024 essay: “Although it will happen incrementally, astounding triumphs – fixing the climate, establishing a space colony, and the discovery of all of physics – will eventually become commonplace.”

But we already know the solution to climate change: reduce greenhouse gas emissions to net zero and the warming will stop. The blockers to doing so, as demonstrated by the recent failure of the COP31 climate summit, are political, not technological. Even if AI were to produce a blueprint for a perfectly functioning nuclear fusion reactor tomorrow, we would still have to build thousands of them across the globe in the next decade or so to avoid the most catastrophic warming effects. In the past decade, we have built 60 nuclear fission reactors, a technology we understand far better than an as-yet-mythical fusion power plant. Again, you can see how AI might offer some improvements, but not enough to counteract our fossil fuel use.

It is important for me to have some humility here, because one thing AI’s breakthroughs in mathematics this year has underlined for me is the need to change my mind when the evidence changes. I started that process with the early signs of AI progress in maths, but didn’t update my beliefs fast enough – though, to be fair to myself, neither did almost everyone else, including leading mathematicians such as Terence Tao, who, just weeks ago, said he didn’t expect the Riemann hypothesis to be solved by AI until 2050.

For that reason, I am on the lookout for early signs that AI success in biology is shifting. That could include an AI-designed drug proving useful in people – for example, Rentosertib, a leading candidate, is now undergoing a phase III trial as a treatment for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a type of lung disease. The trial is expected to conclude in 2029, so we’re talking years of wait for any results. If the drug succeeds, that doesn’t necessarily provide a way for any other AI drug candidates to succeed, and the painfully slow process of molecule selection, animal testing and human trials is still hard to speed up.

If I’m forced to make a prediction, I can fairly confidently state that we will see yet more advances in AI maths in 2027. I also expect that we will see some completely unexpected results in other fields as well. But solving biology? Ending climate change? Defeating disease? These still feel, for now, like science fiction.

articles.personality_title: AI solves major math problems but biology and climate challenges remain complex
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Artificial intelligence (AI) has recently made big progress by solving some of the hardest problems in mathematics. These problems had puzzled humans for many years and required deep thinking and creativity.

**What happened** – In the past year, AI programs have successfully solved difficult math puzzles like the Navier-Stokes problem and the Riemann hypothesis. These achievements surprised many experts because they expected such breakthroughs to take much longer. However, experts caution that AI’s success in math does not mean it will quickly solve complex issues in biology or climate change.

**Impact** – This is important because math problems can be checked and confirmed with clear rules, while biology and climate involve messy, real-world systems that don’t always follow simple logic. For example, diseases like Alzheimer’s involve complicated processes inside the body that are hard to study and understand fully. Climate change is mostly a political and social challenge, not just a scientific one. AI can help, but it won’t solve these problems overnight.

**What's next step** – Researchers will keep using AI to explore biology and medicine, such as testing AI-designed drugs in clinical trials, but results will take years. In math, AI is expected to solve even more difficult problems soon. Scientists are watching closely to see if AI can make real progress in biology and other fields, but patience is needed.

**One-sentence takeaway** – AI has achieved remarkable success in solving tough math problems, but tackling biology and climate change remains a much harder challenge that will take more time and effort.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’IA résout des grands problèmes mathématiques mais la biologie et le climat restent complexes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L’intelligence artificielle (IA) a récemment fait de grands progrès en résolvant certains des problèmes mathématiques les plus difficiles. Ces problèmes ont posé des questions aux humains pendant de nombreuses années et demandaient réflexion et créativité.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Au cours de l’année écoulée, des programmes d’IA ont réussi à résoudre des énigmes mathématiques complexes comme le problème de Navier-Stokes et l’hypothèse de Riemann. Ces succès ont surpris beaucoup d’experts qui pensaient que ces avancées prendraient beaucoup plus de temps. Cependant, les spécialistes préviennent que la réussite de l’IA en mathématiques ne signifie pas qu’elle résoudra rapidement les problèmes complexes en biologie ou en climat.

**Impact** – C’est important car les problèmes mathématiques peuvent être vérifiés avec des règles claires, tandis que la biologie et le climat concernent des systèmes réels compliqués qui ne suivent pas toujours une logique simple. Par exemple, des maladies comme Alzheimer impliquent des processus complexes dans le corps difficiles à étudier. Le changement climatique est surtout un défi politique et social, pas seulement scientifique. L’IA peut aider, mais ne résoudra pas ces problèmes du jour au lendemain.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs continueront d’utiliser l’IA pour explorer la biologie et la médecine, comme tester des médicaments conçus par l’IA dans des essais cliniques, mais les résultats prendront des années. En mathématiques, on s’attend à ce que l’IA résolve bientôt d’autres problèmes difficiles. Les scientifiques surveillent de près les progrès possibles en biologie et dans d’autres domaines, mais la patience est nécessaire.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – L’IA a réussi à résoudre des problèmes mathématiques très difficiles, mais s’attaquer à la biologie et au changement climatique reste un défi beaucoup plus complexe qui demandera plus de temps et d’efforts.
articles.personality_title_es: La IA resuelve grandes problemas matemáticos pero la biología y el clima siguen siendo complejos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La inteligencia artificial (IA) ha avanzado mucho recientemente al resolver algunos de los problemas matemáticos más difíciles. Estos problemas habían desconcertado a los humanos durante muchos años y requerían pensamiento profundo y creatividad.

**Qué pasó** – En el último año, programas de IA lograron resolver acertijos matemáticos difíciles como el problema de Navier-Stokes y la hipótesis de Riemann. Estos logros sorprendieron a muchos expertos porque esperaban que tardaran mucho más. Sin embargo, los especialistas advierten que el éxito de la IA en matemáticas no significa que resolverá rápido problemas complejos en biología o cambio climático.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque los problemas matemáticos pueden verificarse con reglas claras, mientras que la biología y el clima involucran sistemas reales complicados que no siempre siguen una lógica simple. Por ejemplo, enfermedades como el Alzheimer involucran procesos complejos en el cuerpo que son difíciles de estudiar. El cambio climático es principalmente un desafío político y social, no solo científico. La IA puede ayudar, pero no resolverá estos problemas de inmediato.

**Próximos pasos** – Los investigadores seguirán usando IA para explorar la biología y la medicina, como probar medicamentos diseñados por IA en ensayos clínicos, pero los resultados tomarán años. En matemáticas, se espera que la IA resuelva más problemas difíciles pronto. Los científicos están atentos a posibles avances en biología y otros campos, pero se necesita paciencia.

**Resumen en una frase** – La IA ha logrado un éxito notable en resolver problemas matemáticos difíciles, pero enfrentar la biología y el cambio climático sigue siendo un desafío mucho mayor que llevará más tiempo y esfuerzo.

articles.title: The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret
articles.summary: The narwhal’s iconic spiral tusk, once prized in Europe as the horn of a mythical unicorn, conceals an extraordinary feat of natural engineering. Using advanced X-ray technology, an international team of scientists discovered that the tusk contains two intertwined microscopic spirals that twist in opposite directions.
articles.content:
In the 17th century, Danish King Frederik III already knew that the legendary unicorn horn came from a real animal. However, this creature had fins instead of hooves and inhabited the icy waters of the Arctic. The king dispatched an expedition to Greenland to investigate the source of these highly prized objects. The successful mission earned him a throne fashioned entirely from "unicorn horns," enhancing his power and prestige across Europe. Yet the treasured horn was not actually a horn, but "merely" a tooth.

The narwhal's tusk is unlike almost any other tooth in nature. Whereas elongated teeth, including elephant and walrus tusks and beaver incisors, grow in curved shapes, the male narwhal develops a remarkable corkscrew-shaped tooth. Typically, the upper left canine grows forward through the upper lip, twisting counterclockwise as it extends. It can reach two meters (6.6 feet) in length, equivalent to as much as half the animal's body length.

This unusual biological structure caught the attention of an international team of researchers from several scientific disciplines. Using advanced X-ray imaging techniques, they set out to determine whether the arrangement of the tusk's microscopic building blocks could explain the direction of its visible spiral.

What they discovered was even more remarkable than expected. Rather than forming a single spiral, the tusk's tiny structural components create two intertwined helices that twist in opposite directions. Together, they produce an exceptionally stable structure.

The research was conducted at three major European synchrotron facilities: the Swiss Light Source SLS at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen, the MAX IV Laboratory in Lund (Sweden), and the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility ESRF in Grenoble (France). The findings were published in Nature Communications.

A Giant Tooth Built Like Reinforced Concrete

Narwhal tusks continue growing throughout the animals' lives and can easily reach 70 years of age. Despite their striking appearance, the precise purpose of these enormous teeth remains uncertain. Evidence suggests they are primarily involved in mate selection. Narwhals have also been observed crossing their tusks in playful "duels," supporting the idea that the structures are important for reproduction and social interactions.

Although questions remain about how narwhals use their tusks, scientists now have a much clearer picture of how they are constructed.

"Like bones or other teeth in the animal kingdom, the narwhal tusk is a complex composite material whose structure extends from tiny nanoscale building blocks to the visible form of the entire tooth," says Marianne Liebi, a PSI researcher and co-author of the study.

Composite materials combine different substances to achieve properties that the individual components cannot provide alone. Reinforced concrete is a familiar example. Concrete made from cement and sand can withstand considerable pressure, while an internal steel framework helps resist pulling forces and provides additional stability.

"The narwhal tusk, too, must be both hard and flexible," Liebi explains. "Only then can it withstand the strong hydrodynamic forces that swimming generates."

The Remarkable Microscopic Structure of Narwhal Tusks

Most of the narwhal's tusk consists of dentin, the same hard tissue that makes up much of the interior of human teeth. A thinner layer of cementum covers its exterior. In other mammals, cementum is typically confined to the roots of teeth.

Both materials contain extremely fine collagen fibers strengthened by tiny mineral crystals. Much like the steel framework inside reinforced concrete, the collagen fibers provide internal reinforcement, while the mineral crystals supply hardness. This combination allows the tusk to possess both strength and flexibility.

Understanding how this microscopic arrangement produces the much larger spiral presented a significant scientific challenge.

"The collagen fibers and mineral crystals are on the nanometer scale, while the spiral of the tooth only becomes visible at centimeter and meter lengths," Marianne Liebi explains.

A nanometer is one billionth of a meter. To investigate how structures at this incredibly small scale relate to the shape of an entire tusk, the researchers turned to a sophisticated X-ray imaging method known as tensor tomography.

Advanced X-Rays Reveal the Tusk's Hidden Architecture

Conventional dental X-rays produce images because teeth absorb more radiation than the softer tissues around them. The resulting image is essentially a shadow that reveals the shape and density of the tooth.

However, the powerful X-rays generated at synchrotron research facilities can provide far more detailed information. When these beams encounter regularly organized structures inside a material, the X-rays scatter in distinctive patterns. Scientists can analyze those patterns to determine how microscopic components are arranged.

"From these patterns, we can calculate how the nanometer-sized mineralized collagen fibers inside the material are oriented," explains first author Adrian Rodriguez-Palomo.

Rodriguez-Palomo began working on the project while pursuing his PhD at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden. He subsequently continued the research as a postdoctoral researcher at Aarhus University in Denmark.

During tensor tomography, researchers rotate the tooth within the synchrotron's X-ray beam while collecting measurements at individual locations. Millions of these measurements are then combined to reconstruct a three-dimensional representation of the tusk's internal organization, connecting its microscopic components with the much larger structure.

An Unexpected Discovery Hidden in the Data

When the researchers first examined their extensive imaging data, they could not find the spiral structure they had anticipated.

"That puzzled us quite a bit," recalls Marianne Liebi.

Earlier mechanical experiments had indicated that the tusk's characteristic twist should be reflected in the orientation of its collagen fibers and mineral crystals.

"But instead of a helix, all we saw was a regular pattern."

The breakthrough came when the scientists changed their approach. Rather than examining individual points in the three-dimensional images in isolation, they investigated how the orientation of each point related to its neighbors.

"When we compared how these points were oriented relative to each other, a directional trend began to appear," recalls Palomo. "All we had to do then was connect the dots - as in a children's paint-by-numbers kit - and suddenly the structure became visible: two intertwined spirals."

Two Opposing Spirals Give Narwhal Tusks Their Strength

Further examination revealed that the two spirals occupy different regions of the tooth. The thin outer cementum layer forms a left-handed helix, whereas the mineralized collagen structures within the underlying dentin spiral in the opposite direction.

This sophisticated natural design provides substantial mechanical advantages. Much like the intertwined strands of a rope, the two opposing helices work together to create an exceptionally stable structure. Their arrangement helps the tusk resist twisting forces, known as torsion, as well as other forms of mechanical stress.

The same microscopic architecture also produces the narwhal's recognizable corkscrew shape, linking the extraordinary appearance of the legendary unicorn horn to structures far too small to see with the naked eye.

Narwhal Tusks Preserve Decades of Arctic History

The study forms part of a research project funded by NordForsk called "Narwhal tusks - a tale with a twist." It also received support from the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation program under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie program.

Under the leadership of Henrik Birkedal of Aarhus University in Denmark, the international and interdisciplinary research team is exploring both the internal architecture of narwhal tusks and the relationship between tusk growth, environmental conditions, and climate.

As a narwhal's tusk grows, it develops successive layers that function much like the annual growth rings of a tree. Scientists can examine these structures to reconstruct past Arctic environmental conditions, including changes in climate and food availability.

During a lifespan that can approach a century, a male narwhal effectively builds its own environmental archive within its remarkable spiral tooth.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery revealing the unique microscopic structure of narwhal tusks using advanced X-ray imaging. This breakthrough enhances understanding of natural composite materials and has broad implications for biomimetic material science and environmental research, benefiting society's knowledge of nature and potential technological innovations.
articles.personality_title: Scientists uncover the hidden double spiral inside narwhal tusks
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Narwhals are Arctic whales famous for their long, spiral tusks. People once thought these tusks were magical unicorn horns. Scientists have wondered how these tusks grow their unique corkscrew shape.

**What happened** – An international team used powerful X-ray machines at European research centers to look inside narwhal tusks at a tiny scale. They found not one, but two microscopic spirals twisting in opposite directions inside the tusk. These spirals are made of collagen fibers and minerals, creating a strong but flexible structure.

**Impact** – This discovery explains why narwhal tusks are both hard and flexible, able to resist twisting forces when the animals swim or interact. It also links the tusk’s famous spiral shape to tiny details invisible to the naked eye. Understanding this natural design can inspire new materials that combine strength and flexibility, similar to reinforced concrete.

**What’s next step** – Researchers will continue studying how narwhal tusks grow and how their layers record changes in Arctic environments over decades. This could help scientists learn more about climate history and how narwhals survive in their icy habitat.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Narwhal tusks hide a remarkable double spiral structure that makes them strong and flexible, revealing nature’s clever engineering at the smallest scales.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques découvrent la double spirale cachée dans les défenses des narvals
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les narvals sont des baleines de l’Arctique célèbres pour leurs longues défenses en spirale. On pensait autrefois que ces défenses étaient des cornes magiques de licorne. Les scientifiques se demandaient comment ces défenses prenaient cette forme hélicoïdale unique.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe internationale a utilisé des rayons X puissants dans des centres de recherche européens pour observer à très petite échelle l’intérieur des défenses de narval. Ils ont découvert non pas une, mais deux spirales microscopiques qui tournent en sens opposé à l’intérieur de la défense. Ces spirales sont composées de fibres de collagène et de minéraux, créant une structure à la fois solide et flexible.

**Impact** – Cette découverte explique pourquoi les défenses des narvals sont à la fois dures et flexibles, capables de résister aux forces de torsion lorsque les animaux nagent ou interagissent. Elle relie aussi la forme en spirale célèbre de la défense aux détails minuscules invisibles à l’œil nu. Comprendre cette conception naturelle peut inspirer de nouveaux matériaux combinant solidité et souplesse, comme le béton armé.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont continuer à étudier la croissance des défenses et comment leurs couches enregistrent les changements de l’environnement arctique sur plusieurs décennies. Cela pourrait aider à mieux comprendre l’histoire du climat et comment les narvals survivent dans leur habitat glacé.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les défenses des narvals cachent une double spirale remarquable qui les rend solides et flexibles, révélant l’ingénierie ingénieuse de la nature à toute petite échelle.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos descubren la doble espiral oculta dentro de los colmillos de narval
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los narvales son ballenas del Ártico famosas por sus largos colmillos en espiral. Antes se pensaba que estos colmillos eran cuernos mágicos de unicornio. Los científicos querían entender cómo estos colmillos crecen con esa forma de sacacorchos.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo internacional usó potentes máquinas de rayos X en centros de investigación europeos para observar el interior de los colmillos a una escala muy pequeña. Encontraron no una, sino dos espirales microscópicas que giran en direcciones opuestas dentro del colmillo. Estas espirales están hechas de fibras de colágeno y minerales, creando una estructura fuerte pero flexible.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento explica por qué los colmillos de narval son duros y flexibles, capaces de resistir fuerzas de torsión cuando los animales nadan o interactúan. También conecta la famosa forma en espiral del colmillo con detalles muy pequeños que no se pueden ver a simple vista. Entender este diseño natural puede inspirar nuevos materiales que combinen resistencia y flexibilidad, como el concreto reforzado.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores seguirán estudiando cómo crecen los colmillos y cómo sus capas registran cambios en el ambiente ártico durante décadas. Esto podría ayudar a entender mejor la historia climática y cómo sobreviven los narvales en su hábitat helado.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Los colmillos de narval esconden una doble espiral que los hace fuertes y flexibles, revelando la ingeniosa ingeniería natural a las escalas más pequeñas.
